Researchers created two genetically modified versions of L. infantum that each carried different fluorescent markers and drug resistance genes. When sand flies were fed a mixture of these parasites, some offspring inherited both markers and drug resistances, demonstrating genetic exchange between identical strains. These hybrid parasites had three sets of chromosomes (triploid) and remained stable throughout their life cycle, including during infection in mice. Mice infected with the hybrid parasites had much lower

These hybrid parasites had three sets of chromosomes (triploid) and remained stable throughout their life cycle, including during infection in mice. Mice infected with the hybrid parasites had much lower parasite levels in their organs and maintained body weights similar to uninfected mice, indicating less severe disease. The reduced disease severity was linked to lower activity of an enzyme called arginase, which is associated with disease progression. This work confirms that L. infantum can mate within its natural sand fly vector even between genetically identical parasites, producing stable hybrids with slower virulence.
slower virulence.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_text: This study explores how Salmonella genomic island 1 (SGI1), a genetic element carrying multiple antibiotic resistance genes, spreads between bacteria. SGI1 cannot transfer on its own but relies on helper plasmids called IncC plasmids to move between bacterial cells. These IncC plasmids produce a protein complex known as the type IV secretion system (T4SS), which forms a channel that allows DNA to pass from one bacterium to another during conjugation. SGI1 carries three genes similar to parts of this channel, and their expression is activated by the helper plasmid. The proteins made by SGI1 can replace or combine with the plasmid’s own channel components, creating a modified channel that enables SGI1 to transfer more efficiently than the helper plasmid itself.

This study explores how Salmonella genomic island 1 (SGI1), a genetic element carrying multiple antibiotic resistance genes, spreads between bacteria. SGI1 cannot transfer on its own but relies on helper plasmids called IncC plasmids to move between bacterial cells. These IncC plasmids produce a protein complex known as the type IV secretion system (T4SS), which forms a channel that allows DNA to pass from one bacterium to another during conjugation. SGI1 carries three genes similar to parts of this channel, and their expression is activated by the helper plasmid. The proteins made by SGI1 can replace or combine with the plasmid’s own channel components, creating a modified channel that enables SGI1 to transfer more efficiently than the helper plasmid itself.

This study used computer models based on locust brain data to investigate how the insect olfactory system transforms dense, synchronized signals from antennal lobe projection neurons into sparse and specific responses in mushroom body Kenyon cells, which are involved in memory. Before learning, many Kenyon cells responded to odors but with low reliability and less selectivity. The models compared two types of synaptic plasticity at the connections between antennal lobe projection neurons and Kenyon cells: spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which depends on the precise timing of nerve impulses, and spike-rate-dependent plasticity (SRDP), which depends on the overall firing rate. Both plasticity types made Kenyon cell responses sparser and more selective, with fewer neurons responding but more reliably. STDP was more effective

(SRDP), which depends on the overall firing rate. Both plasticity types made Kenyon cell responses sparser and more selective, with fewer neurons responding but more reliably. STDP was more effective at maintaining distinct responses to multiple odors and improving discrimination between similar smells. Plasticity fine-tunes synaptic strengths to enable Kenyon cells to detect synchronized input patterns, which is crucial for accurate and stable odor representation. The findings suggest that experience-dependent changes in synaptic strength help stabilize and sharpen odor coding in the mushroom body, supporting learning and memory. Researchers collected many bacterial samples from human chronic wounds and found that many bacteria had defects in traits linked to causing damage, such as producing proteases, rhamnolipids, motility, and biofilm formation. Using a mouse model of chronic wounds, they tested bacterial mutants lacking specific genes and found that most traditional virulence factors and biofilm formation genes were not needed for bacteria to survive in wounds. The only virulence function affecting bacterial fitness was the type 3 secretion system. Instead, genes involved in anaerobic growth, metabolism, energy production, and maintaining membrane integrity were critical.

targeting biofilm formation or common virulence factors will be effective treatments for chronic wound infections. Instead, therapies that disrupt bacterial metabolism or stress resistance might be more promising. Overall, this work improves understanding of how P. aeruginosa adapts to chronic wounds and highlights new directions for developing treatments.

The researchers developed a mathematical model describing how hypnozoites behave within the liver and validated it using data from tropical strains of P. vivax. Their model shows that the number of hypnozoites varies widely among individuals, with most carrying few or none and some having many, which leads to more relapses and a higher chance of spreading malaria. The model also predicts that standard malaria control methods, such as mosquito control and treatment of blood infections, reduce transmission but may

The model also predicts that standard malaria control methods, such as mosquito control and treatment of blood infections, reduce transmission but may be less effective against P. vivax because of relapses from hypnozoites. Importantly, adding drugs like primaquine that kill hypnozoites in the liver to treatment plans can greatly reduce relapses and transmission. This is because people with many hypnozoites are more likely to relapse and thus receive treatment that clears both blood and liver infections. These findings highlight the importance of targeting the hidden liver stage of P. vivax to improve malaria control and elimination efforts.

Earlier research suggested that during muscle formation, TBP might be replaced by TBP2 to activate muscle genes. However, this study found that TBP2 is not present in muscle cells or muscle stem cells during differentiation, and mice lacking TBP2 show normal muscle repair after injury. Instead, TBP and other parts of the TFIID complex remain present, though at reduced levels, and are necessary for activating muscle genes. When TBP was experimentally reduced in muscle cells, these cells failed to develop properly into muscle fibers,

remain present, though at reduced levels, and are necessary for activating muscle genes. When TBP was experimentally reduced in muscle cells, these cells failed to develop properly into muscle fibers, showing that TBP is essential for muscle gene activation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that TBP, not TBP2, is the critical protein for muscle gene expression during muscle cell differentiation and regeneration.

The researchers identified a key DNA-binding region in PALB2 and showed that mutations in just four amino acids within this region reduce the cell’s ability to repair DNA damage by about half. They also found that this part of PALB2 can promote important DNA repair activities on its own, even without other proteins usually involved in the process. Additionally, PALB2 can work with RNA as well as DNA, suggesting it might

promote important DNA repair activities on its own, even without other proteins usually involved in the process. Additionally, PALB2 can work with RNA as well as DNA, suggesting it might have broader roles in DNA repair linked to gene activity. These findings highlight that PALB2’s ability to bind DNA is essential for effective repair of damaged chromosomes, which helps protect cells from becoming cancerous. Understanding how PALB2 functions could improve knowledge of cancer development and guide future research on DNA repair mechanisms.

Using green fluorescent proteins (GFPs) engineered to have different net charges, the researchers found that in E. coli, proteins with positive charges moved much more slowly—up to 100 times slower—than negatively charged or neutral proteins. This slowdown is mainly caused by positively charged proteins binding to ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines. In Lactococcus lactis and Haloferax volcanii, the effect of positive charge on slowing diffusion was less pronounced, likely because their higher internal salt concentrations reduce these electrostatic interactions. Additionally, how positive charges are spread over the protein surface influences diffusion speed, with uneven

diffusion was less pronounced, likely because their higher internal salt concentrations reduce these electrostatic interactions. Additionally, how positive charges are spread over the protein surface influences diffusion speed, with uneven charge distribution causing slower movement. When cells experienced increased crowding, protein diffusion slowed further. Analysis of the natural proteins in these organisms showed that most cytoplasmic proteins carry negative charges, which may help them avoid slow movement caused by binding to ribosomes. These findings suggest that ribosome surface properties influence which proteins can move efficiently inside cells, affecting overall protein mobility and cellular function.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_text: This study investigated how nerve cells recycle synaptic vesicles (SVs), which are small sacs that store and release chemical messengers for brain communication. When nerve cells are strongly stimulated, SVs release their contents and their membranes are rapidly taken back into the cell through a process called bulk endocytosis, forming large structures known as bulk endosomes. These bulk endosomes then serve as sources for generating new SVs. The researchers studied nerve cells from mice lacking two proteins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, which are important for a common recycling method called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this

called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this reformation was slower. Detailed microscopy showed that clathrin-coated pits appeared only on the cell surface and not on bulk endosomes, and removing clathrin did not further reduce SV recovery. These findings reveal that during intense nerve activity, nerve cells use a recycling pathway that does not require dynamin 1, dynamin 3, or clathrin to regenerate SVs from bulk endosomes. This improves our understanding of how nerve cells maintain communication under high demand and highlights alternative mechanisms for vesicle recycling beyond the well-known clathrin-dependent pathway.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_text: This study investigated how nerve cells recycle synaptic vesicles (SVs), which are small sacs that store and release chemical messengers for brain communication. When nerve cells are strongly stimulated, SVs release their contents and their membranes are rapidly taken back into the cell through a process called bulk endocytosis, forming large structures known as bulk endosomes. These bulk endosomes then serve as sources for generating new SVs. The researchers studied nerve cells from mice lacking two proteins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, which are important for a common recycling method called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this

called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this reformation was slower. Detailed microscopy showed that clathrin-coated pits appeared only on the cell surface and not on bulk endosomes, and removing clathrin did not further reduce SV recovery. These findings reveal that during intense nerve activity, nerve cells use a recycling pathway that does not require dynamin 1, dynamin 3, or clathrin to regenerate SVs from bulk endosomes. This improves our understanding of how nerve cells maintain communication under high demand and highlights alternative mechanisms for vesicle recycling beyond the well-known clathrin-dependent pathway.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_text: During early development, cells divide rapidly without growing, causing them to become smaller with each division. The mitotic spindle, a structure made of microtubules, separates chromosomes during cell division and must adjust its size to fit the shrinking cells. This study used extracts from frog (Xenopus laevis) embryos at different developmental stages to recreate spindle formation in the lab. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane,

by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane, reducing its availability in the cytoplasm and allowing kif2a to become active and reduce spindle size. Changing spindle size in embryos affected how the spindle oriented itself during metaphase but did not disrupt chromosome separation. This work shows that spindle size is controlled by a balance between kif2a and importin α, linked to cell size through the redistribution of importin α between the cytoplasm and membrane. Understanding this mechanism helps explain how cells coordinate internal structures with changing cell size during development.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_text: During early development, cells divide rapidly without growing, causing them to become smaller with each division. The mitotic spindle, a structure made of microtubules, separates chromosomes during cell division and must adjust its size to fit the shrinking cells. This study used extracts from frog (Xenopus laevis) embryos at different developmental stages to recreate spindle formation in the lab. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane,

by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane, reducing its availability in the cytoplasm and allowing kif2a to become active and reduce spindle size. Changing spindle size in embryos affected how the spindle oriented itself during metaphase but did not disrupt chromosome separation. This work shows that spindle size is controlled by a balance between kif2a and importin α, linked to cell size through the redistribution of importin α between the cytoplasm and membrane. Understanding this mechanism helps explain how cells coordinate internal structures with changing cell size during development.

This study used extracts from frog (Xenopus laevis) embryos at different developmental stages to recreate spindle formation in the lab. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane,

by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane, reducing its availability in the cytoplasm and allowing kif2a to become active and reduce spindle size. Changing spindle size in embryos affected how the spindle oriented itself during metaphase but did not disrupt chromosome separation. This work shows that spindle size is controlled by a balance between kif2a and importin α, linked to cell size through the redistribution of importin α between the cytoplasm and membrane. Understanding this mechanism helps explain how cells coordinate internal structures with changing cell size during development.

During early development, cells divide rapidly without growing, causing them to become smaller with each division. The mitotic spindle, a structure made of microtubules, separates chromosomes during cell division and must adjust its size to fit the shrinking cells. This study used extracts from frog (Xenopus laevis) embryos at different developmental stages to recreate spindle formation in the lab. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle.
